title: Navigation Systems and Radar Services
summary: Understand what VOR, DME, GPS, and surveillance displays measure, and what they leave for the pilot to judge.
objectives: Interpret VOR course indications without confusing radial, heading, and TO/FROM.
Explain DME slant range and GPS integrity, sensitivity, and equipment limitations.
Use radar advisories and traffic displays while retaining navigation, weather, and collision-avoidance responsibilities.

sections.title: VOR radials describe position from a station
sections.body:
A VOR supplies angular information referenced to a ground station. A radial is named for the magnetic direction extending from the station. An airplane north of a station is near its 360° radial whether its nose points north, south, or sideways to that line.

Tune the correct frequency, verify the received station identifier by the method approved for the installed equipment, and check operational status and signal validity. A stored database label alone may simply identify the station the receiver expects; some equipment actually decodes and verifies the received identifier. Know the difference.

VHF reception is limited by line of sight, terrain, altitude, and the facility’s service volume. A needle that happens to center does not make an out-of-service or unusable signal suitable for navigation. Check NOTAMs and the published facility information before depending on it.
sections.deep:
The course selected with the OBS defines a line through the station. The CDI then shows which side of that selected line the aircraft occupies. TO/FROM distinguishes the appropriate side of the station relative to the selected course. It does not sense the airplane’s heading or report whether it is presently moving toward the station.

For an airplane north of the station, selecting 180° centers a suitable indication with TO; selecting 360° centers the same geographic line with FROM. Turning the airplane in place does not reverse those flags. Have the student draw the station, aircraft, selected course arrow, and desired direction of travel before discussing which way to correct.

sections.title: CDI sensing: establish the course picture before turning
sections.body:
To track inbound on the north side of a VOR, a pilot would normally select the 180° course with a TO indication, then fly an appropriate intercept heading. To track outbound to the north, select 360° with FROM. In either case, establish the intended course direction and recognize which side of that line the aircraft occupies.

A conventional CDI can give reverse-sensing confusion when the airplane is flown opposite the selected course direction. “Turn toward the needle” is unsafe as a universal rule. First build the geometry, select the intended course correctly, and use the instrument according to its design. An HSI helps display that geometry but still requires correct source and course interpretation.

Apply it: identify the navigation source as well as the needle. A VOR, localizer, and GPS indication may use the same display while measuring different types of deviation.
sections.deep:
VOR deviation is angular. The same angular error corresponds to a smaller cross-track distance close to the station and a larger distance far away. That is why a fixed-size correction made near the station can produce a rapidly moving needle and unnecessary oscillation.

For a small angular error θ, cross-track distance is approximately station distance multiplied by θ in radians. At a 1° angular error, 60 NM corresponds to about 1 NM lateral displacement; 6 NM corresponds to about 0.1 NM. Those are teaching approximations, not receiver tolerances. Near station passage, rapid angular changes and unreliable indications in the overhead region require anticipation rather than aggressive needle chasing.

sections.title: DME measures a slanted line, not the map distance
sections.body:
DME interrogates a ground facility and measures the timing of its replies. The displayed distance is the straight-line slant range from aircraft to station, in nautical miles. It is not automatically horizontal distance to the airport or runway.

When far from a station and relatively low above it, slant range and horizontal distance are close. Over the station at altitude, the display mainly reflects vertical separation. An airplane about 6,000 ft above the DME antenna will still read about 1 NM when directly overhead.

Verify that the distance belongs to the intended, correctly identified facility. Paired VOR/DME channels and combined equipment make tuning convenient, but a familiar-looking distance is not proof that it belongs to the selected airport or localizer. Read the chart and installed-equipment indications.
sections.deep:
The geometry is a right triangle: slant range² = horizontal distance² + height above station², with all three distances in the same units. Height above station is different from altitude MSL. The station elevation must be considered before comparing vertical separation with a charted altitude.

Slant range can also make distance-based groundspeed or time-to-station displays misleading while climbing, descending, or flying across the station rather than directly toward it. A changing distance is a range rate, not necessarily the aircraft’s full groundspeed. Distinguish a DME distance, a GPS distance to a named waypoint, and a remaining-flight-plan distance before using any number in a decision.

sections.title: GPS position and GPS integrity are separate questions
sections.body:
A GNSS receiver uses accurately timed satellite signals to solve for position and receiver-clock error. Four suitable satellites can support a basic three-dimensional position solution. That does not by itself establish that the solution has adequate integrity for an intended operation.

RAIM compares redundant measurements to detect inconsistent data. Conventional unaugmented GPS typically needs at least five satellites for fault detection, or four with suitable barometric aiding. Fault detection and exclusion generally needs six, or five with barometric aiding. Satellite geometry matters as well as count.

WAAS adds corrections and integrity information through a network of reference stations and broadcast links. It is not simply a fixed number of extra satellites. Read the receiver’s actual status and applicable flight-manual supplement. A handheld moving-map position is useful information, but it does not establish approval for an IFR navigation function.
sections.deep:
Four unknowns require four independent measurements: three position coordinates and a clock correction. A fifth measurement creates redundancy, allowing a consistency check. Extra satellites can improve redundancy, but a poor geometric arrangement can still weaken the solution; integrity availability is not guaranteed merely by counting icons.

GNSS interference, signal blockage, database errors, or an incorrectly selected leg can produce different failure modes. A valid satellite solution can still guide the pilot along the wrong programmed course. Cross-check the intended route against independent information and prepare a practical alternative before a loss of navigation becomes urgent. Perform required RAIM predictions and other preflight checks according to the equipment and operation.

sections.title: GPS guidance depends on the active leg and flight phase
sections.body:
A GPS flight plan is a sequence of legs, not merely a list of destinations. Confirm the active leg, its course, the selected navigation source, and whether the receiver is sequencing or holding a leg. “Direct to” can change the route geometry and may bypass intended fixes.

GPS lateral deviation generally represents cross-track distance, unlike a VOR’s angular deviation. The full-scale width can change with operating mode and flight phase. Conventional non-WAAS units commonly use ±2 NM en route, ±1 NM in terminal mode, and ±0.3 NM for an eligible nonprecision approach. Those values are not a universal departure rule or a complete description of modern WAAS approach scaling.

Apply it: interpret the annunciated mode and the aircraft’s approved equipment documentation. A centered needle without the intended source, leg, and scale can be reassuring for the wrong reason.
sections.deep:
At a 0.2 NM cross-track error, a wide en-route scale and a narrow approach scale produce very different needle positions, even though the aircraft has not moved. The sensitivity change is intentional: increasingly precise path control is needed as protected airspace and procedure geometry change.

Approach authorization also depends on procedure loading, database currency, receiver capability, integrity status, and aircraft approval. For an IFR procedure, manually building an approximation from waypoint coordinates does not replace retrieving the approved named procedure when required. For this VFR lesson, the transferable habit is simple: state what the system is commanding, why it is commanding it, and how you would detect a wrong selection.

sections.title: Flight following helps; it does not take over the flight
sections.body:
Request VFR radar advisories with aircraft identification, type, position, altitude, destination, and the service needed. Availability can depend on controller workload, equipment, coverage, and the airspace involved. A discrete code and traffic advisories do not automatically supply clearance into every airspace along the route.

Primary radar can detect reflected energy without a transponder reply. Secondary surveillance uses transponder responses. Mode A provides a code, Mode C adds pressure-altitude reporting, and Mode S supports selective addressing and additional data. ADS-B broadcasts aircraft-derived information rather than waiting for a traditional radar interrogation.

The pilot retains responsibility for navigation, fuel, weather avoidance, terrain clearance, and see-and-avoid as applicable. Advise ATC promptly if an instruction conflicts with maintaining VFR. When assigned a heading, fly the assigned heading rather than substituting the same numeric GPS ground track.
sections.deep:
Controllers see surveillance-derived position and track, but they cannot infer the exact cloud boundary visible out your windshield. Weather displays show selected precipitation information and have limitations; they do not depict all cloud, icing, turbulence, or other hazards. Do not accept a vector into conditions you cannot safely and legally enter.

Use traffic information as a cue for an active visual search. Aircraft may be outside coverage, unequipped, unreported, or filtered from a display. A “no traffic” impression is not a guarantee. Read back and comply with applicable ATC instructions, clarify ambiguity early, and understand when advisory service has terminated or a handoff requires action.

teachBack: Draw a VOR station with an aircraft north of it, then explain centered 180° TO and 360° FROM indications without moving the aircraft.
Show why a DME can read about 1 NM directly over its station.
Explain how a valid GPS position could still guide a pilot along an unintended course.
Demonstrate a concise flight-following request and state which responsibilities stay with the pilot.
takeaways: TO/FROM is about position relative to a selected course, not which way the nose points.
DME, VOR, and GPS measure different geometry; identify the source before interpreting the needle.
A navigation display and an ATC advisory are aids to a pilot’s decisions, not substitutes for them.

quiz.question: An aircraft is due north of a VOR with 180° selected and a centered TO indication. The pilot turns the nose from south to east without changing position. What happens to TO/FROM solely because of the heading change?
options: It changes to FROM
It becomes a GPS indication
It remains TO
It must disappear
feedback: TO/FROM is determined by position and selected course, not the heading alone.
Turning the airplane does not change the selected navigation source.
The aircraft remains on the same side of the station relative to the selected 180° course.
A heading change alone does not invalidate a received VOR signal.
quiz.hint: Ask whether the VOR receiver senses heading as part of this indication.

quiz.question: An airplane is directly over a DME antenna about 6,000 ft below it. What distance should the pilot expect approximately?
options: 0 NM because the map positions coincide
6 NM because the altitude is 6,000 ft
60 NM because altitude must be scaled
1 NM because DME measures slant range
feedback: Horizontal distance is near zero, but vertical separation is still part of slant range.
Six thousand feet is about one nautical mile, not six.
There is no conversion that makes this height sixty nautical miles.
The vertical distance is about one nautical mile and becomes the overhead slant range.
quiz.hint: Convert the height above the antenna to nautical miles.

quiz.question: A non-WAAS receiver can compute a 3D position but reports inadequate integrity for an intended operation. What is the best interpretation?
options: A position solution alone does not establish adequate integrity
The receiver must have no satellites at all
A centered CDI cancels the integrity warning
Selecting direct-to supplies the missing integrity
feedback: The position and its reliability for a particular operation are separate assessments.
A basic solution may exist even when there is insufficient redundancy or geometry for integrity.
Needle position does not override an integrity alert.
Route selection cannot manufacture satellite measurement redundancy.
quiz.hint: Distinguish solving for position from checking that solution.

quiz.question: A GPS CDI becomes more sensitive while the aircraft’s cross-track distance stays unchanged. What most likely changed?
options: The VOR station moved
The receiver’s guidance mode or full-scale width
The airplane’s physical wingspan
Magnetic variation suddenly became zero
feedback: This is a GPS scale question, and a ground station moving does not explain it.
Changing the cross-track distance represented by full-scale deflection changes the needle’s response.
Wingspan does not set navigation CDI sensitivity.
Magnetic variation is unrelated to the full-scale cross-track width.
quiz.hint: Check the mode annunciation and how much distance full-scale represents.

quiz.question: While receiving VFR flight following, a heading assigned by ATC would take the airplane into a cloud. What should the pilot do?
options: Follow it because flight following provides an IFR clearance
Use the same number as GPS track without telling ATC
Maintain safe VFR conditions and promptly advise ATC of the conflict
Assume the cloud is safe because it is absent from ATC weather radar
feedback: VFR advisory service does not supply an IFR clearance or authority to enter cloud.
Substituting track for an assigned heading changes the instruction and leaves the conflict unresolved.
The pilot must retain VFR weather responsibility and communicate an inability to comply safely.
Weather surveillance does not show every cloud or hazard.
quiz.hint: Consider which information is available to the pilot but not necessarily visible to the controller.

quiz.question: The same angular CDI error is observed 60 NM and 6 NM from a VOR. Which statement is correct?
options: The farther position has the larger cross-track displacement
Both represent exactly the same lateral distance
The nearer position is ten times farther from the course line
CDI deflection proves the aircraft’s heading in both cases
feedback: At equal angular error, lateral displacement grows with range from the station.
VOR deviation is angular rather than a fixed cross-track distance scale.
Reducing range by a factor of ten reduces the corresponding small-angle displacement by about ten.
CDI geometry does not directly measure heading.
quiz.hint: Picture two points on the same ray from the station.
